planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in early spring once soil is workable, in full sun with good drainage; stake young trees lightly for the first year since the wood is brittle.

directions: Konstantinopolskaya is an old Eastern European quince cultivar long grown in Ukraine, Moldova, and southern Russia, valued for its large, strongly ribbed, pear-shaped fruit and good cold tolerance compared to Mediterranean quince types. The downy golden-skinned fruit has dense, aromatic flesh that is far too hard and astringent to eat raw but cooks down into richly perfumed paste, jelly, and preserves. Trees are self-fertile, bloom with large pale pink flowers after most frosts have passed, and ripen fruit in mid to late autumn. Because the cultivar tolerates colder winters better than many Turkish or Persian quince selections, it is a reasonable choice for growers at the cooler edge of quince-growing range.

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root trees in early spring in full sun to light shade; Rossica Major tolerates poor, acidic, and cold soils better than most fruiting trees.

directions: Rossica Major is a Russian selection of common rowan chosen for larger, sweeter, less bitter berries than the wild species, making the fruit genuinely worth harvesting for jam, jelly, and traditional fermented preserves after a frost or cooking has mellowed the tannins. The tree bears flat clusters of creamy-white flowers in late spring followed by heavy bunches of orange-red berries that ripen in late summer and persist into autumn, also drawing thrushes and waxwings. It is exceptionally cold-hardy and adaptable to lean, acidic soils where few other fruiting trees thrive, making it a practical choice for northern gardens. Give it an open site with full sun for the heaviest fruit set, though it will still crop reasonably in light shade.
